sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe integumentary structure and function.
- Describe musculoskeletal structure and function.
- Recognize common conditions of these systems.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Your skin is like a big stretchy coat that covers your whole body. It is the biggest covering you have, and nothing else on the outside of you is bigger.

### Question 2

The epidermis is like the top coat of paint on a house: it is the outside layer that gets touched, worn down, and repainted over and over.

### Question 3

The dermis is like the padded filling under the top layer: it holds the blood pipes, the tiny oil and sweat makers, and the roots of your hair.

### Question 4

The hypodermis is like the soft foam pad under a carpet: it keeps you warm and gives a cushion when you bump into things.

### Question 5

Melanin is like built-in sunscreen and paint in one: it gives skin its color and helps block the sun's harsh rays.

### Question 6

Keratin is like the tough plastic coating on a cable: it makes your skin, hair, and nails strong and keeps water from soaking in.

### Question 7

Sebaceous glands are like tiny oil dispensers in your skin that keep your hair and skin from drying out.

### Question 8

When you get hot, your skin is like a radiator turned up high: it lets more warm blood flow near the surface and releases sweat so the air can cool you.

### Question 9

Your skin can make vitamin D when the sun shines on it, like a little factory that turns sunlight into something your bones need.

### Question 10

Your skin is like a strong wall with a moat: germs usually cannot get past it, and the wall even has a slightly sour coating that germs do not like.

### Question 11

The top layer of your skin is like the clear top film on a sticker: it has no pipes carrying blood. The blood pipes are in the layer underneath.

### Question 12

The hair on your head works like a warm hat: it helps keep heat in and shields your scalp from bumps and the sun.

### Question 13

When you are cold, your skin pulls its blood pipes tighter and deeper, like closing the windows of a warm house so the heat stays inside.

### Question 14

As people get older, the skin's stretchy rubber bands and oil supply wear down, so the skin gets drier and looser, like an old elastic band that does not snap back.

### Question 15

A fever is like turning up the thermostat in your house: until the room reaches the new higher setting, the heater kicks on and you feel chilly even though things are warming up.

### Question 16

If a cut looks angry red, feels hot, and oozes yellow goo, that is the body's warning light that germs may have gotten in, so you tell the nurse or doctor right away.

### Question 17

Your skeleton is like the steel frame of a building plus a storage room: it holds you up, shields your soft parts, stores important minerals, and even makes new blood cells.

### Question 18

A grown-up's body has 206 bones, which is like having 206 puzzle pieces that all fit together to make your frame.

### Question 19

The diaphysis is the long middle part of a bone, like the straight body of a dumbbell between the two rounded ends.

### Question 20

The axial skeleton is the center pole of the body: your head, your back stack of bones, and the cage around your chest.

### Question 21

Your skull is like a hard helmet you never take off, guarding the brain inside.

### Question 22

Your ribs are like the bars of a cage that wrap around your chest to keep your heart and lungs safe.

### Question 23

Your backbone is like a tunnel made of stacked rings, and the important nerve highway called the spinal cord runs safely through it.

### Question 24

Red bone marrow is like a blood-cell factory tucked inside your bones, making the cells your blood needs every day.

### Question 25

Your bones are like a savings bank for calcium: they store it away and let some out into your blood whenever your body needs it.

### Question 26

Think of osteoblasts as the bricklayers that add new bone and osteoclasts as the demolition crew that clears away old bone, so your skeleton stays strong and fresh.

### Question 27

A ball-and-socket joint is like a joystick: the round end of one bone sits in a cup, so you can swing your arm or leg in almost any direction.

### Question 28

Your elbow is like a door hinge: it swings open and shut in just one direction instead of moving all around like your shoulder.

### Question 29

Ligaments are like strong rubber bands that tie bones together so a joint stays in place and does not wobble apart.

### Question 30

A tendon is like a strong rope that ties a muscle to a bone, so when the muscle pulls the rope, the bone moves.

### Question 31

Cartilage is like the soft rubber pad on the end of a chair leg: it lets bones slide smoothly without grinding against each other.

### Question 32

Synovial fluid is like oil in a door hinge: it keeps the moving parts slick so they swing easily without squeaking or wearing out.

### Question 33

Skeletal muscle is the muscle you can choose to move, like when you decide to raise your hand or kick a ball.

### Question 34

Smooth muscle works like the automatic walls of a tube that squeeze food through your stomach or push blood along, without you having to think about it.

### Question 35

Cardiac muscle is the special engine of your heart that keeps beating on its own, pumping blood all day and night.

### Question 36

Your biceps and triceps are like a tug-of-war team: when one side pulls and shortens, the other side lets go so the arm can move one way, and they switch for the other way.

### Question 37

Bone is alive, not like a rock: it has its own repair crew that glues the broken pieces back together with new bone over time.

### Question 38

Doctors use a checklist to spot tricky moles, and the B stands for Border: if a mole's edge is wavy or blurry instead of smooth, it is worth a closer look.

### Question 39

If a mole starts growing or changing color, that is the body's warning light, so the best move is to have a doctor look at it soon rather than ignore it.

### Question 40

A first-degree burn is like a mild sunburn: the top layer of skin gets red and sore, then peels and heals on its own.

### Question 41

In a very deep burn, the nerves that feel pain get burned away too, so the spot itself may not hurt even though the burn is very serious.

### Question 42

Athlete's foot is caused by a tiny fungus, like mold, that likes to grow on warm, damp feet.

### Question 43

After someone has chickenpox, the same germ hides out sleeping in their nerves, and years later it can wake up as a painful rash called shingles.

### Question 44

A bedsore happens when one spot of skin is squeezed against a bone for too long, cutting off its blood like a kinked hose, so the skin gets injured.

### Question 45

Cellulitis is when germs get into the deeper skin and make a patch of skin red, hot, and puffy, like an angry red warning zone.

### Question 46

Warts are caused by a tiny virus, not dirt, that makes a little bump grow on the skin.

### Question 47

Acne happens when the skin's oil makers produce too much oil and it plugs up the tiny holes where hairs grow, making bumps.

### Question 48

Psoriasis is when skin cells grow way too fast and pile up into dry, flaky patches, like snow building up on a spot that will not melt.

### Question 49

Eczema makes skin dry, red, and very itchy, like a patch of skin that keeps getting irritated and will not calm down.

### Question 50

In vitiligo, the skin's color-making cells stop working in certain spots, leaving pale patches, like a printer running out of ink in some areas.

### Question 51

Alopecia is the doctor word for losing hair, whether a little or a lot.

### Question 52

Osteoporosis makes bones get spongy and weak, like a bar of soap with holes, so they can break more easily.

### Question 53

To keep bones strong, people need exercise that makes bones work against gravity, plus the building blocks calcium and vitamin D, like giving a house strong bricks and regular use.

### Question 54

Osteoarthritis is like the padding in a hinge wearing out after years of use, so the joint gets stiff and sore.

### Question 55

In rheumatoid arthritis, the body's own defense system gets confused and attacks the joints, while osteoarthritis is more like plain wear and tear from years of use.

### Question 56

Gout happens when a waste product called uric acid builds up and forms sharp little crystals in a joint, like grains of sand in a hinge, causing a painful flare.

### Question 57

A fracture is another word for a broken bone, from a tiny crack to a big break.

### Question 58

A sprain is when the strong rubber bands that tie your bones together get stretched too far or torn.

### Question 59

A strain is when a muscle or the rope that ties it to bone gets pulled too hard, like an overstretched rubber band.

### Question 60

When someone twists an ankle and it is called a sprain, the stretchy bands holding the ankle bones together got pulled too far.

### Question 61

Carpal tunnel happens when a nerve in the wrist gets squeezed in a tight little tunnel, making the hand tingle or go numb.

### Question 62

Scoliosis is when the backbone curves to the side like an S or a C instead of standing straight.

### Question 63

Between each bone in your back is a soft cushion; if it bulges out and pushes on a nerve, it can cause pain, like a squished pillow poking a wire.

### Question 64

Osteomyelitis is when germs get inside a bone and make it infected, which is more serious than a simple bruise.

### Question 65

When you get a cut, your body is like a repair crew: it first plugs the hole with a clot, then sends workers to clean and rebuild the skin over several days.

### Question 66

For a small burn, run cool water over it to calm the skin, and leave any blisters alone so they can protect the healing skin underneath.

### Question 67

If a bone may be broken, the best thing is to keep it as still as possible and get the doctor right away, not to wiggle or push it back into place.

### Question 68

For a twisted ankle, remember RICE: rest it, ice it, wrap it snugly, and prop it up so the swelling goes down.

### Question 69

If a wound gets more red, hot, puffy, and oozes pus, or the person gets a fever, that is the body's alarm bell that germs are winning and a doctor needs to know.

### Question 70

A muscle spasm is like a muscle suddenly squeezing into a tight knot and refusing to let go for a moment.

### Question 71

A DEXA scan is like a special camera that measures how thick and strong your bones are, to see if they are getting weak.

### Question 72

MRSA is a type of tough germ that has learned to shrug off many common medicines, so it needs stronger medicine and careful handling.

### Question 73

If someone hurts their neck in a fall and their arms tingle, that could mean a nerve or the spinal cord is at risk, so they should stay still and get help fast.

### Question 74

If a bone looks bent or out of place after an injury, that is a big red flag that needs a doctor right now, not a wait-and-see appointment.

### Question 75

Dandruff is a mild version of a common flaky-scalp condition, like skin on the head shedding little white flakes.

### Question 76

A dislocation is when a bone pops out of its joint, like a door coming off its hinge.

### Question 77

If a patient's skin or the whites of their eyes look yellow, that is a signal the doctor should know about, so you write it down and tell the care team.

### Question 78

When a muscle sits still inside a cast for weeks, it shrinks like a balloon losing air, which is why doctors have people exercise after the cast comes off.

### Question 79

The fatty layer under the skin is like a slow-release sponge: medicine placed there soaks into the blood gradually instead of all at once.

### Question 80

Sunscreen and a hat are like armor against the sun's harsh rays, helping protect your skin every time you go outside.

### Question 81

When a knee gets hurt and puffs up with swelling, it is like a hinge jammed with debris, so the joint cannot open all the way until it heals.

### Question 82

If someone cannot put weight on their leg after a fall, they should sit down safely and let the doctor know right away, not try to walk it off.

### Question 83

The sun is like a medicine that can also burn: a little helps your body make vitamin D, but too much can hurt your skin, so people balance the good with the risk.

### Question 84

A spreading rash with a fever and trouble breathing is a big alarm: the person needs a doctor's help right away, not a cream.

### Question 85

If someone has back pain and cannot control their bladder or bowels, that is a serious warning sign that needs a doctor right away.
